Where it convinces less is outside the retail context: there you pay for commerce-focused features you barely touch. In practice teams get stuck on the breadth. A platform that wants to be a CDP, personalization, and automation all at once asks for maintenance, and the flows get messy faster than you think. Stevin runs as a layer above Bloomreach, connects it to your CRM and lead sources, and makes sure triggers come from your own data instead of from a loose list, with a person reviewing every action that carries weight first.
bloomreach.stackImpact: Choosing Bloomreach means a CDP, personalization, and automation in one bundle, with the dependence on one vendor for all three. For a webshop that saves loose tools, but use it outside ecommerce and you buy breadth that sits idle. It wants to be both your customer-data source and your activation platform, and that dual role you have to keep an eye on. The practical approach: connect Bloomreach to a real system of record and let it do what it is strong at, personalized commerce, so your customer data does not drift apart in two places.
pitfalls: Using Bloomreach outside ecommerce: you pay for commerce features that sit idle.
Personalization flows that grow organically until no one can oversee them anymore.
Using Bloomreach as the only customer-data source alongside your CRM, so data drifts apart.
Letting triggers come from loose lists instead of from your own data.

blueconic.shortDescription: CDP focused on first-party data and customer profiles.
blueconic.description: BlueConic is a CDP focused on building first-party customer profiles. The platform makes customer data directly available for marketing, personalization, and analytics without relying on third-party data.
blueconic.useCase: Building and activating first-party customer profiles for marketing and personalization.
blueconic.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI uses BlueConic to build first-party customer profiles and connects them to marketing channels for targeted campaigns and personalization.
problemsSolved: Too dependent on third-party data for targeting
No central customer profile based on your own data
First-party data is not used for marketing
blueconic.stevinAngle: BlueConic focuses on first-party customer profiles, and in a world that is saying goodbye to third-party data that is a sensible focus. The platform makes your own customer data directly usable for marketing, personalization, and analytics without leaning on cookies from outside. For teams that want to future-proof their targeting, that is the right angle. Where it pinches: collecting first-party data is one thing, turning it into a complete and usable profile is another. BlueConic builds the profile, but without clean sources and a clear goal it stays a collection of fragments. And a profile does not activate itself. Stevin connects to BlueConic through the API, reads the first-party profiles and behavioral signals, and turns them into concrete follow-up, with the consultant reviewing every action that carries weight first.
blueconic.stackImpact: Choosing BlueConic means betting on your own data instead of on third-party sources, and that requires you to also collect and keep that data clean seriously. It builds central profiles, but the quality hangs entirely on what you put into it. The activation to channels you set up separately, that is not built in ready-made. The practical approach: make sure your first-party data streams hold up first, because a CDP that runs on your own data is exactly as good as the data you bring in yourself.
pitfalls: Collecting first-party data without clean sources, so the profiles stay fragmentary.
Expecting BlueConic to save targeting without your own data streams in order.
Having a central profile without anything activating it in your channels.
Underestimating the shift away from third-party data as purely a tool choice.

bol-com.shortDescription: The largest online marketplace in the Benelux.
bol-com.description: Bol.com is the dominant marketplace in the Netherlands and Belgium. For many webshops it is an important sales channel alongside their own shop.
bol-com.useCase: Selling through Bol.com as an additional channel.
bol-com.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI helps integrate your Bol.com sales into your overall marketing and sales reporting so you have a complete picture of your revenue.
problemsSolved: Bol.com sales sit apart from your marketing data
No integrated overview of all sales channels
bol-com.stevinAngle: Bol.com is the dominant marketplace in the Benelux, and for many webshops a sales channel you cannot ignore. That is the reality and at the same time the tension: you sell on a platform you do not own, with data that stays inside Bol and that you have to pull into your own stack. We run into it at clients where Bol is a serious share of revenue, alongside their own shop. Where teams get stuck is the overview: the Bol sales sit apart from the rest of the marketing and sales data, so you do not have a complete picture of your revenue. Stevin adds a layer on top, pulls the sales data out of Bol through the connection, and brings it together with your other channels, so a person sees what is going on in one place.
bol-com.stackImpact: Choosing Bol.com as a channel means part of your revenue runs on someone else's platform: the data sits in Bol and you have to get it out to put it next to your own shop. Count on a connection to get sales data into your reporting, otherwise Bol stays a blind spot. It is a sales channel, not a marketing stack, so integrating it into your overview is your work. The question is whether you can see your total revenue, or only each channel on its own.
pitfalls: Keeping Bol sales separate from your own shop data, so your revenue picture is incomplete.
Becoming dependent on a channel you do not own without building your own channel.
Not making a connection, so the Bol data stays a blind spot in your reporting.

bol-retail-media.shortDescription: Advertising on bol.com through retail media.
bol-retail-media.description: bol Retail Media lets you promote products on bol.com through sponsored products and display ads. Ideal for brands and sellers who want to grow their visibility on the largest Benelux marketplace.
bol-retail-media.useCase: Promoting products and growing visibility on bol.com.
bol-retail-media.howWeUseIt: Stevin manages bol Retail Media campaigns and connects the results to your broader marketing reporting so you can compare the ROI of retail media against other channels.
problemsSolved: Retail media on bol.com sits apart from your other marketing channels
No view of the total ROI of your media budget including retail media
bol-retail-media.stevinAngle: bol Retail Media puts your products at the top of the largest marketplace in the Benelux, with sponsored products and display inside bol itself. The strength is clear: you advertise at the moment someone is already buying. We use it with brands and sellers who do real volume on bol. Where it pinches is that retail media is its own world, with its own figures, that rarely stands next to your other channels. You see how a campaign performs on bol, but not how it compares to your Google or Meta spend, or what it does to your total margin. Stevin runs as a layer on top of your stack and pulls the bol data in through export, next to your inventory and your other channels. A product that runs well but is nearly sold out, a campaign that eats spend without return: that becomes a signal a person sees in time.
bol-retail-media.stackImpact: Choosing to advertise on bol means you want to be able to place the results next to your inventory and your other channels, because on its own a good ACoS says little about your total picture. You need your product data and your media mix alongside it. The risk is that bol becomes its own little island with its own success figures that nobody compares. In practice: make sure campaigns, inventory and your other spend come into one picture, otherwise you steer on a platform KPI instead of on what your business keeps.
pitfalls: Judging bol campaigns in isolation, so you cannot weigh them against your other channels.
Keeping ads running on a product that is nearly sold out because inventory and campaign are not linked.
Steering on ACoS when the question is what it earns your business overall.

bouw7.shortDescription: Project administration and estimating for construction (Exact Online Bouw).
bouw7.description: Bouw7, part of Exact Online Bouw, is project software for contractors and finishing firms: estimating, planning, time tracking and invoicing at the project level. The data sits in there cleanly, but it does not always reach the right person in time.
bouw7.useCase: Keep projects, estimates and planning in one place, from quote to handover.
bouw7.howWeUseIt: Stevin is built to run as a work layer on top of systems like Bouw7. It reads projects, estimates and planning and turns loose information into signals: a quote that was never followed up, a delivery that has not been confirmed, a planning step that is blocked. Stevin does not replace Bouw7, it makes sure that what is in there reaches the right person in time. You can connect through the API, an export or a mail parser.
problemsSolved: Information is scattered across email, planning and the project software
Quotes and extra work are not followed up in time
A planning step gets stuck without anyone seeing it
No overview of what needs attention per project
bouw7.stevinAngle: Bouw7 handles project administration for contractors and finishing firms solidly: estimating, planning, hours and invoicing all sit neatly at the project level. The data is correct, that is not the problem. The problem is that it stays inside the system while the real work happens in email and on site. We see teams stall on exactly that gap: a quote nobody followed up, extra work that was never confirmed, a planning step that gets blocked without anyone noticing. Bouw7 records all of it, but it taps no one on the shoulder. That is the layer we put Stevin on. Through the API, an export or a mail parser, Stevin reads projects, estimates and planning and turns them into signals with a concrete next action underneath. The project lead sees every action that carries weight first, before anything goes out the door.
bouw7.stackImpact: Choosing Bouw7 means your administration is in order, but the follow-up still has to come from somewhere. In practice that follow-up lives in someone's inbox or in their head, and that scales badly the moment you run more projects at once. The connection runs through the API or an export, so the question is not whether the data comes out, but what happens to it once a quote is left sitting. Count on watching the planning side alongside Bouw7, because the system does not flag on its own when a step stalls.
pitfalls: Assuming that recording data well is the same as following up: the quote keeps sitting there.
Letting follow-up live in the inbox, which falls apart once you run more projects.
Not confirming extra work because no one has a signal set on it.
Only noticing a blocked planning step when the site goes quiet.

bouwvision.shortDescription: ERP and project administration for construction.
bouwvision.description: BouwVision is business software for construction firms: estimating, project administration, purchasing, hours and invoicing in one place.
bouwvision.useCase: Manage the project administration and purchasing of construction firms.
bouwvision.howWeUseIt: Stevin connects to BouwVision and recognizes signals in projects and purchasing: an order that was not confirmed, a budget line that deviates, a project that needs attention. The judgment and the execution stay with the person. Connect through the API or an export.
problemsSolved: Purchasing and project information is scattered
Unconfirmed orders go unnoticed
Deviations in the budget are seen too late
No early signals per project
bouwvision.stevinAngle: BouwVision keeps the project administration and purchasing of construction firms in one place: estimating, project administration, purchasing, hours and invoicing. Solid and complete, but like other ERPs in this corner it is strong at recording and quiet at warning. The purchasing side is where we most often see teams trip up: an order the supplier never confirmed, a budget line that deviates from the estimate, a project that needs attention without anything lighting up. BouwVision knows it, but it only surfaces once someone opens the report. Stevin connects to it through the API or an export and turns purchasing and project data into signals with a next action underneath. The judgment and the execution stay with the person. Stevin makes sure an unconfirmed order or a deviating budget gets noticed in time, not at the delivery or the after-the-fact costing.
bouwvision.stackImpact: BouwVision covers project and purchasing in one, so functionally there is little you need to add. The gain is in the monitoring on top. The connection runs through the API or an export, and the real question is which purchasing and project moments you want to see early: unconfirmed orders, budget deviations, projects that need attention. Without something watching for that, the information waits in a report no one opens daily, and you only see a problem once it is already on the site or in the figures.
pitfalls: Letting an unconfirmed order run until the delivery fails to show up on site.
Only seeing budget deviations at the after-the-fact costing, when correcting is no longer possible.
Leaving purchasing and project information scattered with nothing that pulls it together.
Relying on a report no one opens daily for what needs attention.

branch.shortDescription: Mobile linking and attribution for cross-channel app journeys.
branch.description: Branch is a mobile linking platform with attribution, deep linking, and journey tools. Strong in cross-channel scenarios where web, email, and social need to lead to an app.
branch.useCase: Cross-channel deep linking and mobile attribution.
branch.howWeUseIt: Stevin uses Branch to measure web-to-app journeys and quantify the impact of non-paid channels on app installs and activations.
problemsSolved: The web-to-app journey is not measurable
Deep links break between channels
branch.stevinAngle: Branch solves an annoying problem most tools ignore: deep links that break the moment a user jumps from web to app. It keeps that journey intact and measures what happens, and that is exactly why we use it when web, mail, and social need to lead to an app. Where it is less strong: Branch measures the crossover well, but it is not a full attribution platform and in heavy iOS scenarios you run into the same Apple limits as everywhere. The win is in the linking and the measurement of non-paid channels into the app, not in a complete media picture. Where teams get stuck is that the nice journey data stays sitting in Branch and never carries through into decisions about channels and budget. Stevin reads the Branch data through the API, quantifies what owned and organic contribute to app activations, and turns a notable shift into a signal. A person decides on the follow-up.
branch.stackImpact: Choosing Branch means you can finally follow web-to-app journeys, but you do have to lay it next to your broader attribution to base decisions on it. It is a linking and measurement layer, not a steering instrument, so count on something that translates the numbers into actions. Connect it to your media and CRM data, otherwise you see that a channel leads to app but not what that is worth. The question that remains: who connects this journey data to your budget choices.
pitfalls: Seeing Branch as a complete attribution platform when it mainly does linking and measurement.
Collecting web-to-app journey data without anyone tying channel decisions to it.
Setting up deep links and then not testing them across all the channels they need to work in.
Assuming measuring the crossover is the same as steering the whole journey.

braze.shortDescription: Enterprise customer engagement platform for cross-channel lifecycle.
braze.description: Braze is an enterprise customer engagement platform for email, push, in-app, SMS, and WhatsApp. Widely used by consumer brands and apps with large, differentiated audiences that need to be triggered in real time.
braze.useCase: Cross-channel lifecycle marketing at scale for consumer brands and apps.
braze.howWeUseIt: Stevin integrates Braze with your CDP, product data, and advertising so lifecycle flows are fed by behavioral cohorts and feed into a shared attribution model.
problemsSolved: Lifecycle marketing sits in a silo without media context
Behavioral triggers are not connected to acquisition
No measurable uplift on CRM channels
braze.stevinAngle: Braze is built for consumer brands and apps that want to trigger at scale and in real time across email, push, in-app, SMS, and WhatsApp. It does that well: the speed and the behavioral targeting are stronger than the classic email platforms. We use it for clients with large, differentiated audiences and an app or product that generates enough signals. Where it pinches is the dependence on a clean data stream: without a CDP or product data feeding the cohorts, you fall back on simple segments and pay for power you do not use. Stevin puts a layer over Braze, connects it to your CDP and product data, and watches whether the lifecycle flows still fire on the right cohorts, with a person reviewing every change that carries weight first.
braze.stackImpact: Choosing Braze means you need a reliable source of behavioral data: usually a CDP or a product that sends events. Without that layer it is an expensive sending engine. It covers a lot of channels, so you do not need a separate tool per channel, but the data setup underneath decides whether it pays off. Count on work on the connection to your CDP and your advertising, otherwise lifecycle stays a silo without media context.
pitfalls: Choosing Braze without a CDP or product data: you pay for real-time triggers on cohorts you do not have.
Running lifecycle flows separate from acquisition, so you see the uplift nowhere.
Turning on the channel breadth before the data stream underneath holds up.

brevo.shortDescription: Email, SMS, and marketing automation platform.
brevo.description: Brevo (formerly Sendinblue) offers email marketing, SMS, chat, and marketing automation in one platform at a sharp price.
brevo.howWeUseIt: Stevin implements Brevo as your email and automation platform and connects it to your CRM and lead sources.
problemsSolved: You want affordable marketing automation
Email and SMS are not combined
brevo.stevinAngle: Brevo, formerly Sendinblue, is the choice when price weighs more than depth. Email, SMS, chat, and automation in one platform, at a rate the American players do not come close to. We use it for clients who want multichannel without a Klaviyo budget, and where the flows do not need to be complicated. Where it pinches is the moment you want more than a welcome series: the segmentation and reporting are thinner than the pricier alternatives, and the flows get cluttered fast. That is where we put Stevin. Through the API, Stevin reads your sends and connects Brevo to your CRM and lead sources, so the right trigger comes from your own data instead of a loose list nobody maintains. The person sees every action that carries weight first.
brevo.stackImpact: Brevo covers email and SMS in one, so you do not need a separate SMS tool. But it wants to be your CRM and your marketing platform at the same time, and in that double role it is the best at neither. In practice: connect Brevo to a real CRM and let it do what it is good at, sending. That keeps your contact data from drifting apart across two systems. So count on a separate CRM alongside it once you want to follow up on sales seriously, because otherwise you run into the limits of the segmentation and reporting sooner or later.
pitfalls: Using Brevo as a full CRM: the contact data drifts apart from your real system of record.
Flows that grow organically until nobody knows which trigger fires on what.
Choosing on price and only later noticing the segmentation and reporting are thinner than you need.

bullhorn.shortDescription: CRM specific to the staffing and recruitment industry.
bullhorn.description: Bullhorn is the most widely used CRM in the staffing and recruitment industry. It combines candidate management, CRM, and operational processes.
bullhorn.useCase: CRM and candidate management for staffing and recruitment agencies.
bullhorn.howWeUseIt: Stevin connects Bullhorn to your recruitment campaigns so applicants and leads land in the right process automatically.
problemsSolved: Leads from recruitment campaigns are not processed automatically
No connection between advertising and candidate management
bullhorn.stevinAngle: Bullhorn is the standard in staffing and recruitment, and that is no accident: it combines candidate management, CRM, and operational processes in a way built specifically for the industry. We recommend it over generic CRMs the moment recruitment is the core of the business, because a general system misses the logic of candidate and vacancy side by side. The flip side of that specialization: Bullhorn is built for the industry, not for speed or modern marketing connections. It can feel clunky, the interface looks dated, and it does not integrate with your ad channels on its own. Where teams get stuck is that leads and applicants from recruitment campaigns do not land in the right process automatically, and that advertising and candidate management sit apart. Stevin connects to Bullhorn through the API, moves candidates from campaigns into the right process, and turns an applicant left without follow-up into a signal. The person reviews every intervention first.
bullhorn.stackImpact: Choosing Bullhorn means you bring in an industry-specific system that understands exactly the recruitment logic of candidate and vacancy, but the marketing connections do not come on their own. Count on advertising and candidate management sitting apart until you build that bridge, otherwise you process campaign leads by hand and momentum leaks out of your recruitment. It is not a tool you make light for fun, the strength sits in the depth for recruitment and that calls for setup. In practice: let Bullhorn carry the recruitment process and put a layer on top that routes campaign leads into the right track automatically and watches that they get follow-up.
pitfalls: Processing leads from recruitment campaigns by hand because advertising and Bullhorn are not connected.
Assuming an industry-specific system also brings modern marketing connections.
Letting an applicant sit without follow-up because nothing raises the signal.
Confusing the dated interface with a system that does not do its job: the depth sits underneath.

canva.shortDescription: Accessible design tool for fast ad variations and templates.
canva.description: Canva makes it possible to produce professional visuals without a design background. With Brand Kit and Magic Design it is ideal for teams that iterate fast on ad variations.
canva.useCase: Fast production of ad variations and social content.
canva.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI combines creative recommendations with Canva's template system. The creative team gets specific instructions (color palette, composition, copy) that can be executed straight in Canva.
problemsSolved: Creative production is a bottleneck in the campaign cycle
Not every team member can work in Adobe
Ad variations do not get tested systematically
canva.stevinAngle: Canva is the honest choice for teams without a design department. With Brand Kit and Magic Design, someone with no background can knock together a tidy-looking variant, and that is exactly the value: speed and accessibility, not depth. Where it pinches is once volume grows. You easily make twenty variants, but Canva does not tell you which one works, and without that feedback it becomes repeating a pattern you thought was good. Teams stay stuck there: lots of output, little direction. Stevin runs as a layer over that process. It reads which creatives convert in your ad channels, turns that into a concrete instruction (this color palette, this layout, this copy), and lays it next to the work in Canva. That way the next variant comes from data instead of taste, with a person seeing the instruction first.
canva.stackImpact: Canva covers production for anyone who does not need Adobe, so it saves you time and license costs there. But it stops at the design: whether a variant works is not something it teaches you. Count on a link between your ad performance and your creative production, otherwise you never test systematically and keep guessing. In practice: let Canva do what it is good at, making things fast, and pull the direction from your real results. That keeps production from replacing the thinking.
pitfalls: Mistaking volume for progress: twenty variants without knowing which one works.
Setting up Brand Kit and assuming consistency is the same as effectiveness.
Making ad variants without a link that tests which one converts.
Iterating on taste because Canva feeds back no performance.

census.shortDescription: Reverse ETL for enterprise warehouse-to-app data syncs.
census.description: Census is a reverse ETL platform that syncs data from Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and Redshift to 200+ business tools. Strong in enterprise environments with strict governance requirements.
census.useCase: Operationalizing warehouse data in marketing, sales and support tools.
census.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI uses Census for governance-friendly audience activation and data syncs to advertising and CRM, with the logic staying in the warehouse.
problemsSolved: Audience activation bypasses enterprise governance
Data logic gets duplicated in every vertical tool
census.stevinAngle: Census is reverse ETL for the enterprise: data from Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks or Redshift to hundreds of business tools, with a strong emphasis on governance. Where lighter reverse ETL tools stop at simple syncs, Census is built for environments with strict compliance requirements, and that is exactly the reason to choose it over an alternative. The gain is that data logic stays in the warehouse instead of duplicating itself in every vertical tool. Where teams get stuck is the idea that governance-friendly activation also handles the thinking for them. Census syncs reliably, but what you sync and why stays human work. Stevin deploys Census for audience activation and data syncs to advertising and CRM with the logic in the warehouse, and reads the activated segments to put signals and follow-up underneath, with a person reviewing every action that carries weight first.
census.stackImpact: Choosing Census means audience activation stays inside your governance instead of running around it, and data logic stays in one place instead of in every tool separately. That is valuable in compliance-heavy environments, but it requires a mature warehouse and documented models as a base. In practice: keep the transformation logic in the warehouse and use Census purely to activate, because the moment you let logic leak back into the tools you lose the governance advantage you paid for.
pitfalls: Assuming governance-friendly activation also handles the segment logic for you.
Letting data logic leak into the tools after all, so the governance advantage evaporates.
Deploying Census without a mature warehouse as a reliable base.
Confusing reverse ETL with a complete CDP including modeling.

channable.shortDescription: Product feed management and shopping ad optimization.
channable.description: Channable is one of the largest feed management platforms in Europe. It optimizes product feeds for Google Shopping, Meta, Amazon, and hundreds of other channels. Rules decide which products get advertised where and how titles and descriptions get adjusted.
channable.useCase: Product feed optimization, multi-channel shopping ads, and dynamic ads.
channable.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI links campaign performance to Channable's feed rules. Products that waste budget (high spend, zero conversion) get flagged automatically. The Advisor generates feed optimizations based on real performance data instead of manual rules.
problemsSolved: Feed rules get managed manually without performance context
Budget wasters in shopping feeds get discovered too late
No link between product performance and feed prioritization
Multi-channel feed management takes too much manual work
channable.stevinAngle: Channable is one of the heavyweights in feed management in Europe, and rightly so: it sends your product feed to Google Shopping, Meta, Amazon, and hundreds of channels, with rules that decide what appears where and how titles get adjusted. As an engine to keep feeds clean and multi-channel, it is strong. The limit is that the rules stay manual and know nothing about performance. A rule changes a title, but does not know whether a product is burning money, and in practice you discover a budget leak only once it has been running for weeks. Teams get stuck there: the feed is technically correct, but the prioritization sits apart from what actually sells. Stevin links your campaign performance to Channable's feed rules. It reads via API which products soak up budget without converting, flags that, and proposes feed adjustments that rest on real results instead of handiwork. The consultant approves every change with impact.
channable.stackImpact: Channable handles the distribution of your feed across all your channels, so you save a lot of manual work there. But it operates on rules, not results: it does not know which product pays off. Count on a layer that feeds your shopping performance back into the feed prioritization, otherwise you keep optimizing on assumptions and discover budget wasters too late. The feed enters the channels clean, the real question is whether the right products get the attention and the budget. Without that feedback you steer blind.
pitfalls: Managing feed rules manually without performance steering them.
Only discovering a budget waster in the feed once it has been running for weeks.
Letting the feed be technically correct while the prioritization sits apart from what sells.
Not feeding shopping performance back into which products deserve budget.

faqs.question: Does Stevin.AI replace Channable?
faqs.answer: No. Channable stays the feed engine. Stevin.AI adds the intelligence layer: which products to switch on or off, which titles perform better, where budget leaks away.

close.shortDescription: Call-focused CRM with built-in calling and recording.
close.description: Close is a CRM built for call-heavy sales teams: built-in calling, recording that ties to the contact, plus email and SMS in one place. Strong for cold acquisition with two or more people.
close.useCase: A CRM for teams that call a lot and want every conversation tied to the right contact.
close.howWeUseIt: Stevin runs as an AI layer over Close. Through the REST API and webhooks, Stevin reads conversations, leads, and pipeline and delivers follow-up: the draft after a call, and the signals about what is going wrong before it shows up in the reports. Close does the calling, Stevin the thinking on top.
problemsSolved: Calling, recording, and CRM sit apart from each other
Follow-up gets left after a call
No signal before a deal cools off
close.stevinAngle: Close is built for teams that call all day, and you can tell: calling, recording, and CRM sit in one place instead of three tabs. That is exactly why we use it with call-heavy clients and do not recommend a generic CRM with calling tacked on. What Close does not do is think about what should happen after a call. The recording ties neatly to the contact, but the draft email, the next action, and the signal that a deal is cooling off before it shows up in the reports, that stays human work. That is where we put Stevin. Through the REST API and webhooks, Stevin reads every conversation and delivers the follow-up underneath, with the consultant seeing the draft before it goes out. Close does the calling, Stevin the thinking on top.
close.stackImpact: Close is strong when your whole sales process runs around the phone. Choose it for a team that works mainly through email and forms, and you pay for calling features you barely use. It keeps conversations, leads, and pipeline in one place, so you do not need a separate calling tool. The question that remains is what happens with all those conversations after they are recorded.
pitfalls: Choosing Close when your team rarely calls: you pay for the core function sitting idle.
Recordings that pile up without anyone turning them into a next action.
Assuming a tied recording is the same as follow-up.

cm-com.shortDescription: Dutch platform for conversational commerce and messaging.
cm-com.description: CM.com is a Dutch platform for messaging, payment solutions, and conversational commerce. It offers SMS, WhatsApp Business, chatbots, and ticketing in one platform.
cm-com.useCase: Customer communication via SMS, WhatsApp, and messaging channels.
cm-com.howWeUseIt: Stevin connects CM.com to your CRM and marketing automation so messaging channels become part of your automated customer communication.
problemsSolved: Messaging channels are not integrated with the CRM and automation
No automated follow-up via WhatsApp or SMS
cm-com.stevinAngle: CM.com is Dutch and strong where messaging and payments come together: SMS, WhatsApp Business, chatbots, and ticketing in one platform, with a serious payment arm underneath. We use it for clients who genuinely want to run conversational commerce, mainly on WhatsApp, and who value a local party. Where teams get stuck is the expectation that the messaging channels slot into their process on their own. CM.com sends and receives cleanly, but what should happen with an incoming message, and when an automated follow-up should start, that stays setup work. Stevin runs as a layer over CM.com, connects the messaging channels to your CRM and your marketing automation, and turns incoming signals into concrete follow-up, with the person seeing and approving every action that carries weight first.
cm-com.stackImpact: Choosing CM.com means you have messaging and payments in one place, so for WhatsApp and SMS you do not need a separate tool. But it is not a CRM and not a full automation suite, so you connect it to your system of record and your lead process, otherwise the channels stand apart. Count on setting up the connections. The question is not whether you can send a message, but whether the follow-up after it kicks off automatically.
pitfalls: Turning on WhatsApp without it being connected to your CRM: incoming messages get left sitting.
Running messaging as a standalone channel instead of as part of your lead process.
Assuming an incoming message leads to follow-up on its own.

commercetools.shortDescription: Headless commerce platform for flexible ecommerce.
commercetools.description: commercetools is a headless commerce platform that works through APIs. It offers maximum flexibility for companies that want to develop their ecommerce front end and back end independently.
commercetools.useCase: Headless ecommerce with maximum flexibility and scalability.
commercetools.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI connects commercetools to your tracking, product feeds, and marketing channels so your headless setup is fully linked to your marketing stack.
problemsSolved: Tracking in a headless commerce setup is complex
Ecommerce data does not reach the marketing tools automatically
commercetools.stevinAngle: commercetools is a headless commerce platform that works entirely through APIs: you develop the front end and back end separately, with maximum flexibility and scale as a result. That is a deliberate choice for teams that really want to build, and the wrong one for anyone expecting a ready-made shop. We run into it at larger organizations with a development team and requirements a standard platform cannot handle. Where teams get stuck is the measurement side: in a headless commerce setup tracking is complex, and ecommerce data does not reach the marketing tools on its own. An order in the back end does not land in your analysis by itself. Stevin adds a layer on top, reads order and product data through the API, and turns anything that looks off into signals and follow-up, with a person reviewing every action that carries weight first.
commercetools.stackImpact: Choosing commercetools means you buy control and scale and that you build the entire presentation and measurement layer yourself: it delivers the commerce API, not a ready-made store. Count on serious development work for the front end, the tracking, and the connections to your marketing stack. Out of the box, ecommerce data does not end up in your tools. The gain sits in the flexibility, as long as you have the capacity to build it and keep it measured. Without that, it stays a powerful engine with no dashboard.
pitfalls: Going headless commerce without a development team to build the front end and measurement layer.
Underestimating tracking: in an API-first setup nothing falls into place on its own.
Leaving order and product data sitting in the back end with no connection to your marketing tools.

consentmanager.shortDescription: European consent management platform for GDPR compliance.
consentmanager.description: consentmanager is a European consent management platform with extensive configuration options and support for IAB TCF. It is aimed at publishers and advertisers who need full GDPR compliance.
consentmanager.useCase: GDPR-compliant consent management with IAB TCF support.
consentmanager.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI implements consentmanager and makes sure it works correctly with your tracking, Google Consent Mode and advertising platforms.
problemsSolved: Consent management does not meet IAB TCF standards
Tracking and consent are not correctly aligned
consentmanager.stevinAngle: consentmanager is the choice when you genuinely need IAB TCF: a European platform with a lot of knobs, built for publishers and advertisers who have to demonstrate strict, standardized consent. We use it where the advertising ecosystem expects those TCF signals and a simple banner falls short. At the same time, that depth is also the risk: a lot of configuration means a lot that can sit wrong, and TCF makes the chain between banner, tags and advertising platform a good deal more sensitive. Teams get stuck when the TCF string is built up neatly but the measurement does not connect to it. consentmanager handles the consent, not whether your tracking is correct afterward. Stevin runs on top, reads the consent status with your tag data and flags when measurement drops out or a tag ignores consent, so a misconfiguration surfaces before your advertising and reporting suffer underneath.
consentmanager.stackImpact: Choosing consentmanager means stepping into the TCF world, with all the connections that come with it: tag manager, Consent Mode and the advertising platforms that expect the string. That is exactly why you take it, but also where it can break. In practice: set up the whole chain in one go and verify that the TCF signals come through correctly everywhere. The question that remains is not whether you are TCF compliant, but whether your measurement and advertising actually respond to what is in that consent.
pitfalls: Building the TCF string correctly but not connecting the measurement to it.
Choosing consentmanager without genuinely needing TCF.
Setting the many configuration options and then not testing whether everything comes through.
Connecting advertising platforms that interpret the TCF signals differently.

contentful.shortDescription: Headless CMS for flexible content delivery.
contentful.description: Contentful is a headless CMS that delivers content to any front end through APIs. A good fit for companies that want to publish content across multiple channels.
contentful.useCase: Headless content management for multichannel publishing.
contentful.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI connects Contentful content to your marketing stack and makes sure tracking and personalization work correctly in a headless setup.
problemsSolved: Tracking in a headless setup is complex
Content and marketing data are not connected
contentful.stevinAngle: Contentful is a headless CMS: it delivers content to any front end through APIs, which is ideal if you want to publish across multiple channels. That is a deliberate choice with a price, because headless means you build the entire presentation and data layer yourself. We run into it with clients who genuinely publish multichannel and have a development team. Where teams get stuck is the measurement side: in a headless setup tracking is more complex than on a classic CMS, and content and marketing data easily drift apart. A change to the content does not land in your analysis on its own. Stevin adds a layer on top, reads the relevant events through the API, and keeps content and behavior tied together, with a person seeing every change that carries weight first.
contentful.stackImpact: Choosing Contentful means you split content and presentation: powerful for multichannel, but you build the front end and the measurement layer yourself. Count on development work to get tracking reliable, because in a headless setup it does not fall into place on its own. It is a content API, not a marketing platform, so you connect it to your analytics and CRM. The question is not whether you can show content everywhere, but whether you can still measure what happens with that content.
pitfalls: Going headless without a development team to build the front end and tracking.
Letting content and marketing data drift apart, so you cannot tell what performs.
Assuming tracking in a headless setup is as simple as on a classic CMS.

contentsquare.shortDescription: Enterprise digital experience analytics: heatmaps, sessions, journeys.
contentsquare.description: ContentSquare is an enterprise digital experience platform with session replay, heatmaps, journey analysis, and frustration scoring. Widely used by retail, finance, and B2B organizations that take a systematic approach to UX optimization.
contentsquare.useCase: UX analysis, frustration detection, and journey optimization at enterprise scale.
contentsquare.howWeUseIt: Stevin connects ContentSquare insights to campaigns and landing page optimization so UX findings carry straight through into conversion and media strategy.
problemsSolved: UX insights stay stuck in a tool of their own
Frustration on landing pages is not tied to media spend
contentsquare.stevinAngle: ContentSquare is strong at one thing most tools do only on the surface: seeing where visitors get stuck. Session replay, heatmaps, and frustration scoring let you actually watch someone struggle with a page, and that is worth more than bare conversion numbers. We use it with clients who take UX seriously and do not want to keep running on gut feel. Where it pinches is this: ContentSquare shows you there is a problem, but fixes nothing and does not tie its insights to your media spend. The findings stay stuck in a tool that analysts open and the rest of the company does not. An expensive landing page that frustrates visitors costs you money you see nowhere. Stevin reads the signals out of ContentSquare through the API and lays them next to your campaign data, so a frustration spike on a page you are sending ad budget to becomes a concrete action. A person reviews every intervention first.
contentsquare.stackImpact: Choosing ContentSquare means you bring in a lot of insight, but you have to build the bridge to your media and your conversion yourself. It is an analysis tool, not an action tool, so count on the findings needing handwork before they change anything. Connect it to your ad data, otherwise you know a page frustrates people but not how much budget you are sending to it. The question that remains: who picks up the finding and makes sure it lands in the media strategy before it is forgotten.
pitfalls: UX findings that stay stuck in the tool and never touch a page or campaign.
Not tying frustration on a landing page to the media spend going to it: you pay for traffic that bails.
Watching replays without a process to actually carry the fix through.
Assuming seeing a problem is the same as solving it.

cookiebot.shortDescription: Cookie consent management for GDPR compliance.
cookiebot.description: Cookiebot is a widely used consent management tool that makes sure your website complies with GDPR. It automatically scans cookies and manages consent.
cookiebot.useCase: Cookie consent and privacy compliance for your website.
cookiebot.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI implements Cookiebot and connects it to Google Consent Mode so your tracking automatically adapts to each visitor's consent status. That way you measure compliantly without needless data loss.
problemsSolved: Website is not GDPR compliant
Tracking does not work well together with consent
Data loss from consent that is too strict or wrongly configured
cookiebot.stevinAngle: Cookiebot does one thing well: it scans your site, finds the cookies and puts a banner over the top that looks tidy to the regulator. We use it for clients who need to be demonstrably compliant fast without standing up a whole privacy project. Where it pinches is the connection to your measurement. A banner that sits too strict or does not talk to Consent Mode quietly costs you conversion data, and you only notice that weeks later in a report that does not add up. Cookiebot handles the consent, but it does not watch whether your tracking still works afterward. That is where Stevin sits on top. Through the consent status and your tag data, Stevin flags when measurement drops out because of consent, so a broken setup surfaces before a whole month of data is unusable, with a person confirming the fix.
cookiebot.stackImpact: Cookiebot covers the consent part, but it does not handle your measurement. Count on a tag manager alongside it and a correct Consent Mode v2 connection, otherwise your banner sits right but your data still leaks away. It does scan your cookies, but it says nothing about the quality of what still comes in after consent. In practice: configure Cookiebot and your tags as one whole, not as two separate projects, and test whether your core conversions survive the banner. The question that remains is not whether you are compliant, but whether you have enough reliable data left after consent to steer on.
pitfalls: Setting the banner too strict without Consent Mode: you lose measurable conversions without noticing.
Installing Cookiebot separately from your tag manager, after which tags ignore consent.
Assuming a placed banner equals correct measurement.
Accepting a faulty scan, so cookies are missing from the banner.

copernica.shortDescription: Dutch email and marketing automation platform.
copernica.description: Copernica is a Dutch marketing automation platform with strong email, SMS, and database functionality. It offers advanced segmentation and personalization based on your own data models.
copernica.useCase: Advanced email marketing and automation with flexible data models.
copernica.howWeUseIt: Stevin implements Copernica and connects it to your CRM and lead sources for automated, personalized email campaigns and follow-up.
problemsSolved: Email campaigns are not personalized on customer data
Automation is not connected to the CRM or lead sources
You want a Dutch platform with local support
copernica.stevinAngle: Copernica is Dutch, and you notice it in the support and in how it handles data: you build your own data model and drive your email and SMS off it. For teams that want advanced segmentation on a custom data structure, that is strong, and the local line is just the difference for a lot of clients. Where it pinches is the learning curve: the flexible data model is also the hard part of it, and without someone who sets it up well it quickly becomes a system only a few people understand. We use Copernica where the personalization really has to run on customer data. Stevin puts a layer over that: it connects Copernica to your CRM and lead sources through the API, so the right data feeds into the data model and the follow-up holds up, with a person reviewing every action that carries weight first.
copernica.stackImpact: Choosing Copernica means investing in the setup: the data model is powerful, but you have to get it right, otherwise the personalization snags on messy fields. It is not a CRM, so you keep your system of record alongside it and make sure the data stays in sync. It covers email and SMS, so a separate SMS tool is not needed. The gain is in what you put into the data model, not in the platform itself.
pitfalls: Letting the data model be built by someone who will soon be gone: then nobody understands the structure anymore.
Letting customer data in Copernica drift from your CRM, so personalization runs on stale fields.
Confusing the flexibility with speed: without a good setup, every change costs time.

copper.description: Copper is a CRM that is fully integrated with Google Workspace. It works from Gmail and Google Calendar and is ideal for teams already working in the Google ecosystem.
copper.useCase: A CRM for Google Workspace users.
copper.howWeUseIt: Stevin connects Copper to your marketing tools and makes sure leads from campaigns are created automatically as contacts in your Google environment.
problemsSolved: The CRM feels like an extra system alongside Google Workspace
Leads are not synced automatically
copper.stevinAngle: Copper has a strong premise: a CRM that lives fully inside Google Workspace. It works from Gmail and Calendar, so a team that already sits in Google all day does not have to jump to a separate system. For Workspace users it feels less like an extra tool and more like a natural extension. The limit sits in exactly that dependency. Copper is built around Google, and outside that ecosystem it loses its main argument. It is not a deep sales platform for heavy pipelines, and anyone who does not run Workspace has little reason to choose it. Where teams get stuck is that the CRM starts to feel like an extra system after all and that leads are not synced automatically. Stevin connects to Copper through the API, creates campaign leads automatically as contacts in your Google environment, and turns a stalling deal into a signal with a concrete action. The person sees every action that carries weight first.
copper.stackImpact: Choosing Copper mainly makes sense if your whole team sits in Google Workspace, because that is where the value comes from and where it feels like an extension of Gmail. If you do not run on Google, there are stronger CRMs ready and you miss the only distinguishing argument Copper has. It is light in design, so for heavy sales pipelines with many stages and forecasting it gets tight and you hit the limits. In practice: worthwhile inside Google Workspace, and put a layer on top that syncs leads and guards the follow-up so nothing gets left.
pitfalls: Choosing Copper without Google Workspace: then its main reason to exist falls away.
Stretching a lightweight CRM into a heavy sales pipeline it cannot handle.
Assuming living in Gmail is the same as automatically synced leads.
Expecting Google integration to also mean deep sales functionality.

creativex.shortDescription: Creative quality scoring and brand consistency at scale.
creativex.description: CreativeX automatically scores every ad on creative quality: is the brand visible in the first 3 seconds? Does the format meet platform best practices? Is the branding consistent? Essential for brands that produce hundreds of ads per month.
creativex.useCase: Creative quality assurance, brand compliance, and platform-specific optimization.
creativex.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI integrates CreativeX scores into the publishing process. Ads that fall below quality thresholds get flagged automatically before they get budget. The result: higher average creative quality and less budget wasted on bad ads.
problemsSolved: No scalable way to measure creative quality
Brand guidelines get applied inconsistently across markets and teams
Platform best practices are not followed systematically
Bad creatives get the same budget as good ones
creativex.stevinAngle: CreativeX does one specific job well: at scale, it scores whether an ad has the basics in order. Is the brand on screen in the first seconds, does the format fit, is the branding consistent. For anyone running hundreds of ads a month, that is a useful sieve. But mind the assumption: meeting the rules is not the same as performing. CreativeX measures compliance, not conversion, and an ad can follow every best practice and still do nothing. Teams get stuck there: the score is green, the result stays out. Stevin lays the quality score next to your real performance. It reads CreativeX via API and links the compliance score to what the ad delivers in your channels, so you do not just flag what fails the guideline, you also see what meets the guideline and still wastes budget. A person decides what gets paused or scaled.
creativex.stackImpact: Choosing CreativeX means you can finally guard creative quality at a scale where a person can no longer keep up. But it judges on form, not result, so you need your ad performance next to it to give the score meaning. Count on a layer that brings compliance and conversion together and puts the combination into your publishing process, otherwise you block ads that break the rules but work, and let through ads that are tidy and deliver nothing. The score is a sieve, not a verdict on return, and that distinction has to be guarded somewhere.
pitfalls: Mistaking a green quality score for proof that an ad performs.
Guarding compliance without laying the score next to your real conversion.
Blocking ads that break the guideline but sell.
Letting budget keep running on ads that are tidy and still deliver nothing.

criteo.description: Criteo specializes in retargeting and dynamic display ads. The platform uses machine learning to show personalized ads based on earlier behavior.
criteo.useCase: Dynamic retargeting for e-commerce and lead generation.
criteo.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI implements the Criteo pixel and product feeds and makes sure retargeting campaigns connect to your broader marketing funnel.
problemsSolved: Retargeting is not tied to current product data
No insight into how much extra value retargeting actually adds
criteo.stevinAngle: Criteo does one thing well and has done for a long time: dynamic retargeting with product ads that adapt to what someone viewed. For e-commerce with a product feed it usually delivers tidy results. The honest story is that a large part of those results is retargeting, and retargeting easily claims conversions that would have happened anyway. We see webshops stall on this: Criteo's reporting looks strong, but the feed is out of date so the wrong products get shown, and no one can say how much of that revenue was genuinely extra. The platform optimizes within its own screen, not on your broader funnel. Stevin runs as a layer on top, reads the campaign and feed data through the API and flags where the feed is off or where the retargeting figures are mostly claiming existing conversions. The person judges, Stevin keeps the channel honest against the rest of the mix.
criteo.stackImpact: Choosing Criteo requires a clean, current product feed, because without that it shows the wrong products and the return drops without you noticing right away. Count on a connection between your webshop, your feed and your analytics. The pixel and the feed handle the data flow, so the numbers do come out. The hard question is how much of that claimed revenue was genuinely extra and would not have happened anyway. Without something that lays the channel next to your other sources, you may be paying for conversions you would have had regardless.
pitfalls: Running on an out-of-date feed, then Criteo shows the wrong products and the return drops.
Believing the platform's reporting without checking how much revenue was genuinely extra.
Judging retargeting apart from the funnel, so blind to double-counting with other channels.
Assuming a strong dashboard is the same as a strong contribution.

customer-io.shortDescription: Event-driven marketing automation for SaaS and tech.
customer-io.description: Customer.io is a marketing automation platform that triggers on user behavior and events. Popular with SaaS companies and tech firms.
customer-io.howWeUseIt: Stevin implements Customer.io with the right event tracking and connects it to your product and marketing data for personalized automation.
problemsSolved: Automation is not based on user behavior
No connection between product data and marketing
customer-io.stevinAngle: Customer.io is built for teams that want to trigger on behavior, not on a static list. You fire an email off an event in your product, and it does that well: the behavioral segmentation and the message builder are stronger than the cheaper platforms. We use it for SaaS and tech clients where the value sits in the product data. Where teams get stuck is the assumption that the tool itself supplies the events. It does not: without a clean event layer from your product, you get flows firing on nothing, and then you are mostly sending empty messages. Stevin runs as a layer over Customer.io and watches whether the right events come in and whether a flow still does what it should, with the person seeing every change that carries weight first.
customer-io.stackImpact: Choosing Customer.io means you need a reliable event source: your product has to send the right signals, otherwise the platform sits idle. Count on work on the tracking layer, not just the email. It is not a CRM, so your sales data stays in your real system of record and you connect it alongside. The question is not whether you can build pretty flows, but whether the data underneath holds the moment an event fires.
pitfalls: Starting flows before your event tracking is reliable: you send messages on signals that are wrong.
Wanting to use Customer.io as a CRM: it is a sending engine, not a system of record.
Stacking behavioral triggers until nobody can see who gets which message and why.

databricks.shortDescription: Lakehouse platform for enterprise data, AI and analytics.
databricks.description: Databricks is an enterprise lakehouse platform that combines data warehousing and data science. Widely used by large organizations for central storage, ML models and BI in one place.
databricks.useCase: Enterprise data lakehouse for analytics, ML and marketing data.
databricks.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI integrates with Databricks to run marketing data, MMM output and attribution models on your central data layer, without pulling data out of your governance perimeter.
problemsSolved: Marketing data sits apart from the enterprise data layer
MMM models run on separate exports instead of the source of truth
No governance on marketing analytics workloads
databricks.stevinAngle: Databricks is a lakehouse platform that brings data warehousing and data science together, and for large organizations it is often the central place where storage, ML models and BI come together. That is what makes it strong: your marketing analytics can run on the same layer as the rest of the business, inside the same governance. The strength is also the barrier: Databricks is a platform for data teams, not a marketing tool, and without that expertise you get little out of it. Where teams get stuck is that marketing data stays separate from the enterprise layer, that MMM models run on separate exports instead of the source of truth, and that marketing analytics falls outside governance. Stevin integrates with Databricks to run those models on the central data layer without pulling data out of the governance perimeter, and turns the output into signals with follow-up, with a person reviewing every action that carries weight first.
databricks.stackImpact: Choosing Databricks means your marketing analytics runs on the enterprise foundation instead of on loose exports next to your central data. That keeps governance in one place, but it takes data engineering and data teams to get value out of it. It is not an out-of-the-box marketing solution, and without that expertise you get little from it. In practice: run MMM and attribution on the source of truth instead of on copies, because every export outside Databricks is a place where your numbers quietly drift apart from reality.
pitfalls: Keeping marketing data separate from the enterprise layer, so governance and analytics diverge.
Running MMM models on separate exports instead of on the source of truth.
Approaching Databricks as a marketing tool without the data engineering it requires.
Letting marketing analytics fall outside governance and losing reliability with it.

datafeedwatch.shortDescription: Feed optimization and multi-channel product data management.
datafeedwatch.description: DataFeedWatch optimizes product feeds for 2000+ shopping channels. With rule-based transformations and A/B testing of product titles, you can measure the impact of feed changes.
datafeedwatch.useCase: Feed optimization, shopping channel management, and product title testing.
datafeedwatch.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI combines DataFeedWatch's feed optimization with campaign performance data. The Advisor suggests which product titles and descriptions perform better based on click-through and conversion data.
problemsSolved: Product titles are not optimized for search behavior
Feed management across multiple channels takes too much time
The impact of feed changes is not measurable
datafeedwatch.stevinAngle: DataFeedWatch optimizes feeds for a lot of channels and has a strong point many feed tools lack: you can A/B test product titles and measure the impact of a change. That lifts feed work from guessing to testing. The limit is not in the tool, but in what is missing around it. The test shows that title A clicks better than title B, but whether that click also converts and turns a profit sits in your campaign data, not in DataFeedWatch. Teams get stuck there: they optimize for click-through and lose sight of conversion. Stevin combines DataFeedWatch's feed optimization with your campaign performance. It reads both via API and proposes which titles and descriptions deliver not just more clicks but more revenue, so a feed change rests on the whole funnel. The consultant sees the proposal before it goes live.
datafeedwatch.stackImpact: DataFeedWatch covers feed optimization across many channels and gives you real testing options, so it is more than a pass-through. But it measures up to the click: what happens after that sits in your ad and webshop data. Count on a link that brings conversion back to your title tests, otherwise you optimize at the wrong end of the funnel. The gain is in feed tests that do not stop at CTR but run through to revenue. Without that link you pick the title that clicks best, not the title that sells the most.
pitfalls: Optimizing product titles on click-through and losing sight of conversion.
Declaring a title test the winner on the click without the revenue alongside.
Not bringing the conversion data back to your feed tests.
Optimizing at the wrong end of the funnel.

deep-social-listening.shortDescription: Organic signals from forums, communities, and the open web.
deep-social-listening.description: Not all the conversation about your brand happens on your own channels. Deep Social Listening scans forums, communities, and the open web for mentions, sentiment, and trending topics.
deep-social-listening.useCase: Reputation management, sentiment monitoring, and trend detection.
deep-social-listening.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI continuously scans the web for mentions of your name, tracks, or brand. Negative sentiment is flagged right away, positive momentum is turned into Advisor action items.
problemsSolved: You do not know what is being said about you outside your own channels
Negative threads or reviews are discovered too late
Positive buzz is not turned into marketing actions
deep-social-listening.stevinAngle: Not everything said about your brand happens on your own channels. Most of it does not. Deep Social Listening scans forums, communities, and the open web for mentions, sentiment, and what is starting to take hold, and that is exactly the blind spot most brands have: they look at their own replies and miss the conversation already running elsewhere. Strong at finding, weak at following up. A negative thread swelling or a touch of positive buzz is a signal, but without something acting on it, it stays a line in a report. Stevin runs as a layer over the listening layer, catches mentions, and flags negative sentiment right away, while positive momentum is turned into a concrete action item. Anything with impact passes a person first, before a reply or a campaign follows.
deep-social-listening.stackImpact: Social listening delivers volume, and volume means noise, so count on work to separate the mentions that matter from the rest. Sentiment analysis is never perfect, so treat the score as direction, not truth. On its own it is a stream of alerts with no priority, and that is where brands get stuck. So you need something that triages and ties it to your own channels, so an emerging thread does not sink under a hundred irrelevant mentions. In practice: let the listening tool catch, and let a layer on top decide what deserves attention and what is noise.
pitfalls: Drowning in mentions because nothing separates the relevant from the irrelevant.
Taking the sentiment score as fact when it lacks context and can be wrong.
Picking up negative threads too late because there is no direct flag on them.

deployteq.description: Deployteq (formerly Clang) is a Dutch marketing automation platform with strong email, SMS, and cross-channel capabilities.
deployteq.useCase: Cross-channel marketing automation for the Dutch market.
deployteq.howWeUseIt: Stevin implements Deployteq as part of your marketing stack and connects it to your CRM, webshop, and ad channels.
problemsSolved: You want a Dutch platform with local support
Cross-channel automation is not set up
deployteq.stevinAngle: Deployteq, formerly Clang, is a Dutch marketing automation platform with strong email, SMS, and cross-channel options, plus local support that works in your time zone and your language. For clients who value a platform that knows the Dutch market, that is a real edge over the American players. The other side: local support and market knowledge do not always make the platform itself the most modern one. The interface and the way you build flows feel less polished than the big international names, and without someone who knows it, cross-channel scenarios quickly become a maze. Where teams get stuck is that the cross-channel automation is possible but never set up, and that the triggers come from loose lists instead of your real data. Stevin runs as a layer over Deployteq, connects it to your CRM and lead sources through the API, and makes sure the right trigger comes from your own data. A person reviews every campaign that carries weight first.
deployteq.stackImpact: Choosing Deployteq means you bring in a Dutch platform with local support, but setting up cross-channel flows takes work and knowledge. Expect the automation not to stand up on its own: you have to build it and hang it off your data. Without a connection to your CRM, triggers come from loose lists that nobody maintains, and relevance drains away. In practice: let Deployteq do the sending and make sure the right trigger comes from your real data instead of a static list.
pitfalls: Buying cross-channel automation and never actually setting it up.
Letting triggers come from loose lists instead of your current data.
Assuming local support is the same as a platform that builds your flows for you.
Flows that grow organically until nobody knows which trigger fires on what.

didomi.shortDescription: Consent management platform focused on user experience.
didomi.description: Didomi is a consent management platform focused on a good user experience and high opt-in rates. It offers a Preference Center where users can manage their preferences in detail.
didomi.useCase: Consent management with optimized user experience and opt-in rates.
didomi.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI implements Didomi and connects it to Google Consent Mode and your tag management so tracking adapts correctly to the consent status.
problemsSolved: Low consent rates from poor user experience
Consent management is not connected to tracking
No detailed Preference Center for users
didomi.stevinAngle: Didomi aims at the user experience: a tidy banner, a real Preference Center where people can set their choices per category, and as a result a better opt-in. We choose it where the privacy choice has to be visible and well presented, not tucked away in a gray pop-up. The flip side is that a nice Preference Center easily draws the attention and the connection to your tracking gets shortchanged. A detailed choice your tags do not pick up is still data loss. That is where teams get stuck: the banner looks good, but the passthrough to Consent Mode is just slightly off. Stevin runs on top of the consent status from Didomi and your tag data, and raises a signal when a choice does not come through or measurement drops out. That way the gap between what the visitor chose and what your tags do becomes visible, before it pollutes your data.
didomi.stackImpact: Didomi delivers the banner and the Preference Center, but you need a tag manager and a correct Consent Mode connection to make the detailed choices actually work. The finer your consent categories, the more can go wrong in the passthrough. In practice: set up the Preference Center and your tags together and test whether each category actually lands in the measurement. Otherwise you offer visitors choices your system quietly ignores, and that only shows up when your report has odd gaps.
pitfalls: Making the Preference Center nice but not testing the connection to your tags.
Offering many consent categories without checking whether each choice comes through.
Confusing a high opt-in with measurement that really works.
Adding tags that do not follow the fine-grained consent logic.

discord.shortDescription: Community management, server analytics, and fan engagement.
discord.description: Discord is the place for your most engaged fans. Server activity, member growth, and channel engagement are indicators of your community's health.
discord.useCase: Community health monitoring and direct fan engagement.
discord.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI monitors your Discord server metrics and signals when community engagement rises or falls, so you can step in on time.
problemsSolved: No overview of community growth and engagement trends
Important signals in Discord get missed in the flood of information
discord.stevinAngle: Discord is where your most engaged fans sit, and that makes it a more honest gauge than a follower count that mostly looks big. Server activity, member growth, and which channels are alive say something about the health of your community instead of your reach. The problem is familiar to anyone running an active server: information streams past so fast that the signals drown in it. A community cooling off, a recurring complaint, a chance to launch something to your hardest fans, it all gets lost in the noise. Discord measures little and summarizes nothing. Stevin runs as a layer over your server data and signals when engagement rises or sinks, so you can step in on time instead of noticing afterward that it went quiet. You set the action, the person reviews it.
discord.stackImpact: Discord offers an API and bots, but the built-in analytics are thin, so real insight means opening up and storing the data yourself to see trends. It is a community channel, not a measurement system, so count on having to infer your server's health from raw activity yourself. On its own, a busy server tells you little without something keeping the line over time. So the question is not whether people are talking, but whether you notice when it gets quieter, because that is the moment to step in before the community sinks.
pitfalls: Mistaking busyness for health, when it is the falling line you want to catch.
Relying on the thin built-in stats instead of storing the data yourself.
Missing signals in the stream through the sheer volume of messages.

distrokid.shortDescription: Music distribution, royalty tracking, and release management.
distrokid.description: DistroKid distributes your music to all streaming platforms. Royalty data and distribution overviews are essential for your financial planning as an artist.
distrokid.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI integrates DistroKid royalty data with your streaming analytics for a complete financial picture of your music career.
problemsSolved: Royalty data sits apart from your streaming performance data
No overview of earnings per platform per track
distrokid.stevinAngle: DistroKid does one thing well and cheaply: getting your music onto every streaming platform and reporting the royalties back. For most independent artists that is exactly enough, and the price makes it an easy choice. Where it stops is the bigger financial picture. The royalty data sits apart from your streaming performance, so you see what comes in but not how it relates to your growth, and the overview of earnings per platform per track you have to piece together yourself. So your career stays a matter of feel financially while the numbers are right there. Stevin ties the DistroKid royalties to your streaming analytics, so income and listening behavior come into one picture and you see per track and per platform what it earns. Whatever stands out, a track that jumps out financially or one that lags, surfaces as a signal. The choice of what to do with it stays with you.
distrokid.stackImpact: DistroKid gives you royalty reports, but no broad API, so count on exports to get the data out, and on delay because royalties only come in weeks after the streams. The numbers sit apart from your streaming analytics, so for the link between income and listening behavior you need both. On its own it is a payout overview with no context. In practice: line the royalties up per track and platform against your streaming data and let a layer on top pull out the standout outliers, so your financial picture and your growth come into one view instead of two loose exports.
pitfalls: Looking at royalty data apart from streaming performance, so you do not see what growth earns.
Forgetting that the numbers come in delayed, so you draw a wrong current picture.
Not building an overview per track per platform, so outliers go unnoticed.

dpg-media.shortDescription: Premium advertising through Ad Manager across Dutch and Belgian media brands.
dpg-media.description: DPG Media is one of the largest media groups in the Benelux, with brands like AD, Volkskrant, Nu.nl, Libelle and Het Parool. Through their own Ad Manager platform (an alternative to Google Ad Manager) you buy directly against first-party data and premium inventory. This includes Seamless Ads, which run 5 to 10 times higher CTR than standard banners.
dpg-media.useCase: Premium reach on Benelux media brands through display, video, native and Seamless Ads.
dpg-media.howWeUseIt: Stevin connects DPG Media Ad Manager campaign data to your full marketing stack. Results from premium publisher campaigns get combined with your performance channels for a complete attribution picture, including how awareness carries through to downstream conversions.
problemsSolved: Premium media buying sits apart from your performance channels
No integrated view across publisher-direct and programmatic
Publisher first-party data goes unused in your attribution
dpg-media.stevinAngle: DPG Media gives you direct access to premium inventory and first-party data on brands like AD, Volkskrant and Nu.nl through its own Ad Manager, with Seamless Ads that outperform standard banners. If you want to advertise on quality and context in the Benelux, that is a strong card. The catch is not in the placement, it is in the measurement. Publisher-direct campaigns easily end up sitting apart from your performance channels, and the publisher's first-party data is rarely used in your own attribution. We see advertisers get stuck here: premium reach that feels good, but that you cannot show carrying through to conversions. The platform delivers quality, not the proof. Stevin runs as a layer on top, connects the campaign data to your stack through the API, and places publisher-direct next to your performance channels. That way you see how awareness carries through, with a person reviewing the conclusion first.
dpg-media.stackImpact: Choosing DPG Media gives you premium reach and first-party data, but it sits inside its own Ad Manager that is separate from your performance stack. Count on a connection that brings publisher-direct and programmatic together into one attribution picture, otherwise they stay two worlds. The data comes available through the API. The real question is whether the awareness you buy here can be shown carrying through to downstream conversions. Without that integrated picture you judge premium media on feel, while the first-party data is exactly what gives you the chance to prove it.
pitfalls: Leaving publisher-direct separate from your performance channels, so you end up with two split worlds.
Leaving the publisher's first-party data unused in your own attribution.
Judging premium reach on feel without measuring how it carries through to conversions.
Looking at direct and programmatic separately without one integrated view.

dragonfly-ai.shortDescription: Attention prediction for all content: from packaging to digital ads.
dragonfly-ai.description: Dragonfly AI predicts visual attention on any form of content: ads, packaging, in-store displays, websites, and social posts. The platform scores content on saliency and provides heatmaps that show where the eye goes first.
dragonfly-ai.useCase: Cross-channel visual attention analysis and design optimization.
dragonfly-ai.howWeUseIt: Stevin.AI uses Dragonfly AI for clients where the visual impact reaches beyond digital ads, think FMCG with packaging design or retail with shop-window displays. The digital and physical worlds get analyzed the same way.
problemsSolved: Visual attention analysis is limited to digital channels
Packaging design does not get tested for shelf impact
No uniform metric for visual effectiveness across channels
dragonfly-ai.stevinAngle: Dragonfly AI has a wider reach than most attention tools: it predicts where the eye goes on everything, from a digital ad to packaging or a shop window. For FMCG and retail, where the visual impact does not stop at the screen, that is a real difference. The nuance is that it predicts saliency, not sales. A heatmap shows where attention lands, but whether that attention leads to a purchase is a different question. Teams get stuck there: attention gets confused with effect. Stevin uses Dragonfly where physical and digital meet and links the saliency results via API to what actually happens afterward in your channels and your sales data, so a design choice does not just stand out but also delivers. Every recommendation with impact goes past a person first.
